about: Chapter 1, We the Travellers I: 59 patterns, three or four for each of the 15 skills (1 and 2 marks), three 3-mark and three 5-mark long answers in steps (#208), and three 4-mark case studies, drawn from the chapter's 500 questions. All DRAFT until Ashalatha approves them; the first five were sent to her as samples on 27 Oct 2026.

patterns.text: Continue the pattern: {start:num}, {start + step:num}, {start + 2 * step:num}, ___.
patterns.hint: Find how much the numbers go up by each time.
patterns.explanation: The numbers go up by {step:num} each time, so the next one is {start + 2 * step:num} + {step:num} = {start + 3 * step:num}.
patterns.misconception: Looks only at the last digit or repeats visible digits without checking a constant change.
patterns.notes: start: 1,000 to 95,000, a multiple of 50. step: 10, 50, 100, 250 or 1,000.

values.name: ans
values.expr: t1 if pos == 1 else (t2 if pos == 2 else t3)

patterns.text: Find the missing number in the pattern: {s1:num}, {s2:num}, {s3:num}, {t4:num}.
patterns.hint: Find how much the numbers change each time, using two numbers that are next to each other.
patterns.explanation: The numbers go {'up' if dir == 1 else 'down'} by {step:num} each time, so the missing number is {ans:num}. The pattern is {t1:num}, {t2:num}, {t3:num}, {t4:num}.
patterns.misconception: Looks only at the last digit or repeats visible digits without checking a constant change.
patterns.notes: Four terms with the first, second or third missing (never the last: that is P1). Step 25 to 2,000; the pattern goes up or down; every term from 1,000 to 99,999.

patterns.text: What is the rule for the pattern {t1:num}, {t2:num}, {t3:num}, {t4:num}?

wrong.mistake: reads the change one place too low
takes the change across two steps instead of one
gets the direction of the pattern wrong

patterns.hint: Subtract the first number from the second, then check the next pair.
patterns.explanation: {max(t1, t2):num} − {min(t1, t2):num} = {rule.s:num}, and the numbers keep going {'up' if dir == 1 else 'down'} by the same amount. So the rule is: {rule.add if dir == 1 else rule.sub}.
patterns.misconception: Looks only at the last digit or repeats visible digits without checking a constant change.
patterns.notes: Steps 50, 200, 250, 300, 500, 900, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000 or 2,500; going up or down; every term from 1,000 to 99,999. Wrong rules: a tenth of the step, double the step, the opposite direction.

patterns.text: The odometer of a {vehicle} reads {start:num} km. The reading goes up by {per} km each day. What will it read after {days} days?

steps.text: Adds it to the first reading: {start:num} + {total:num} = {start + total:num} km.

patterns.hint: Find the total increase for {days} equal days first.
patterns.explanation: The increase is {per} × {days} = {total:num} km. The new reading is {start:num} + {total:num} = {start + total:num} km.
patterns.misconception: Looks only at the last digit or repeats visible digits without checking a constant change.
patterns.notes: Start reading 10,000 to 85,000 km (a multiple of 10); 45 to 495 km a day (a multiple of 5, not of 100); 3 to 8 days. The answer stays below 99,999 and is in km, stated in the question.

patterns.text: Which number has {a} ten-thousands, {b} thousands, {c} hundreds, {d} tens and {e} ones?
patterns.hint: Write each digit in its named place. Write 0 for a place with nothing in it.
patterns.explanation: Writing the digits {a}, {b}, {c}, {d}, {e} in their places from ten-thousands to ones gives {a * 10000 + b * 1000 + c * 100 + d * 10 + e:num}.
patterns.misconception: Drops internal zeroes or places commas after every three digits from the left.
patterns.notes: All five places named; at least one of the thousands, hundreds and tens digits is 0 (but not all three), so the zero placeholder is tested. No place has exactly 1 (avoids "1 tens"); ten-thousands and ones 2 to 9.

patterns.text: Which numeral is {th.w} thousand {r.w}?

wrong.mistake: puts the last part one place too far to the left
leaves out a zero placeholder and writes only four digits
writes the last part in the wrong place

patterns.hint: Write {th.w} thousand first, then fill the hundreds, tens and ones places.
patterns.explanation: In numerals, {th.w} thousand is {th.n * 1000:num} and {r.w} is {r.n}. Together they make {n:num}, with 0 in the empty places.
patterns.misconception: Drops internal zeroes or places commas after every three digits from the left.
patterns.notes: Thousands part from 24 word forms (twelve to ninety-nine thousand); the last part is a single digit (one to nine) or a tens word (twenty to ninety), so the hundreds place (and often the tens) is 0.

patterns.responseFormat: Two integers separated by a semicolon
patterns.text: A railway office prints two ticket numbers: (a) {th.w} thousand {wa}, and (b) {th.w} thousand {wb}. Write both as numerals.

steps.text: (a) writes {th.n * 1000 + va:num}, keeping the zero placeholders.
(b) writes {th.n * 1000 + vb:num}, with the {dd.d} in the {'tens' if kind == 1 else 'hundreds'} place.

patterns.hint: Both numbers start with {th.n * 1000:num}. Check which place the last part goes in.
patterns.explanation: In numerals, {th.w} thousand is {th.n * 1000:num}. (a) {wa} is {va}, so {th.n * 1000 + va:num}. (b) {wb} is {vb}, so {th.n * 1000 + vb:num}.
patterns.misconception: Drops internal zeroes or places commas after every three digits from the left.
patterns.notes: Same thousands part (twelve to ninety-nine thousand) for both; the last parts use the same digit 1 to 9 as ones and tens, ones and hundreds, or tens and hundreds, so only careful zero placeholders separate them.

patterns.text: What is the place value of the digit {d} in {n:num}?

wrong.mistake: gives the face value instead of the place value
reads the place one too high
reads the place one too low

patterns.hint: Which place is the digit {d} in?
patterns.explanation: The {d} is in the place worth {place:num}, so its value is {d} × {place:num} = {d * place:num}.
patterns.misconception: Confuses a digit's face value with the value created by its position.
patterns.notes: n: 10,000 to 99,999. The digit asked about is in the ten-thousands, thousands or hundreds place, is not 0, and appears once in n.

require: pl.p == 100 or digit(n, pl.p) != digit(n, pl.mirror)
count_digit(n, digit(n, pl.p)) == 1 or digit(n, pl.p) == 0
patterns.text: Which digit is in the {pl.w} place of {n:num}?
patterns.hint: Start at the right with ones and move left: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands.
patterns.explanation: In {n:num}, the places are {digit(n, 10000)} ten-thousands, {digit(n, 1000)} {'thousand' if (digit(n, 1000)) == 1 else 'thousands'}, {digit(n, 100)} {'hundred' if (digit(n, 100)) == 1 else 'hundreds'}, {digit(n, 10)} {'ten' if (digit(n, 10)) == 1 else 'tens'} and {digit(n, 1)} {'one' if (digit(n, 1)) == 1 else 'ones'}. The {pl.w} digit is {digit(n, pl.p)}.
patterns.misconception: Confuses a digit's face value with the value created by its position.
patterns.notes: n: 10,000 to 99,999; asks for the ten-thousands, thousands, hundreds or tens digit. That digit differs from the one in the mirror place (so counting from the wrong end gives a different answer) and appears only once (0 may repeat).

values.name: thing
choice: A visitor counter at a fort

patterns.text: {thing} changes from {n:num} to {m:num}. By how much did the number increase?

wrong.mistake: subtracts the face values of the changed digits only
gives the place value of the new digit, not the change
reads the changed place one place off

patterns.hint: Find the one place where the digit has changed.
patterns.explanation: Only the {'ten-thousands' if p == 10000 else ('thousands' if p == 1000 else ('hundreds' if p == 100 else 'tens'))} digit changes, from {a} to {b}. Its value goes from {a * p:num} to {b * p:num}, an increase of {(b - a) * p:num}.
patterns.misconception: Confuses a digit's face value with the value created by its position.
patterns.notes: n: 10,000 to 99,999. One digit (ten-thousands, thousands, hundreds or tens place, not 0) goes up to a bigger digit; nothing else changes.

patterns.text: The digit {d} appears twice in {n:num}. What is the difference between the place values of the two {d}s?

steps.text: Gives the two place values: {d * pp.hi:num} ({pp.hiw}) and {d * pp.lo:num} ({pp.low}).
Subtracts: {d * pp.hi:num} − {d * pp.lo:num} = {d * pp.hi - d * pp.lo:num}.

patterns.hint: Each {d} has a different value because it is in a different place.
patterns.explanation: The {d}s are in the {pp.hiw} and {pp.low} places, so they stand for {d * pp.hi:num} and {d * pp.lo:num}. The difference is {d * pp.hi:num} − {d * pp.lo:num} = {d * pp.hi - d * pp.lo:num}.
patterns.misconception: Confuses a digit's face value with the value created by its position.
patterns.notes: n: 10,000 to 99,999 with one non-zero digit appearing exactly twice, in any two places; the other three digits are different from it.

patterns.text: Write {t1:num} + {t2:num} + {t3:num} + {t4} in standard form.
patterns.hint: Put each part in its own place. Write 0 for the place that is missing.
patterns.explanation: {t1:num} + {t2:num} + {t3:num} + {t4} = {n:num}. There are no {'thousands' if z == 1000 else ('hundreds' if z == 100 else 'tens')}, so that place is 0.
patterns.misconception: Writes zero-value places as extra digits or assumes each place can have only 0–9 groups.
patterns.notes: A five-digit number with exactly one of the thousands, hundreds or tens places empty (0); the other digits 1 to 9. Parts are given in order from ten-thousands to ones.

patterns.text: Find the number: {a} thousands + {h} hundreds + {t} tens + {o} ones.

wrong.mistake: writes the group counts side by side without regrouping
keeps only the ones digit of the hundreds count and loses the thousands inside it
regroups the hundreds into thousands but forgets the hundreds left over

patterns.hint: {h} hundreds equal {h * 100:num}.
patterns.misconception: Writes zero-value places as extra digits or assumes each place can have only 0–9 groups.
patterns.notes: 2 to 9 thousands, 11 to 29 hundreds (not 20), 2 to 9 tens and ones, so the hundreds must be regrouped.

patterns.text: Complete: {n:num} = {s1} ten-thousands + {s2} thousands + {s3} hundreds + {r} ones.
patterns.hint: Work out the value of the groups you know and subtract it from {n:num}.
patterns.explanation: The known groups make {known:num}. {n:num} − {known:num} = {rest:num}, which is {ans} {unitw}.
patterns.misconception: Writes zero-value places as extra digits or assumes each place can have only 0–9 groups.
patterns.notes: n: 20,000 to 99,999, last two digits 10 or more. Either one ten-thousand is regrouped into the thousands (blank is 10 to 19 thousands) or one thousand into the hundreds (blank is 10 to 19 hundreds); every other group in the sum is 2 or more (never 0 or 1).

values.name: ans
values.expr: lo if da < db else hi

patterns.text: Which is closer to {target:num}: {lo:num} or {hi:num}? Enter the closer number.
patterns.hint: Find how far each number is from {target:num}.
patterns.explanation: {lo:num} is {da} away, while {hi:num} is {db} away. So {ans:num} is closer.
patterns.misconception: Compares only the first visible digit rather than number of digits and left-to-right place value.
patterns.notes: Target 20,000 to 90,000 (a multiple of 10,000); one number 50 to 950 below it and one 50 to 950 above it (multiples of 50, never the same distance). Either may be the closer one.

values.name: la
values.expr: n1 if perm.a == 1 else (n2 if perm.a == 2 else (n3 if perm.a == 3 else n4))

values.name: lb
values.expr: n1 if perm.b == 1 else (n2 if perm.b == 2 else (n3 if perm.b == 3 else n4))

values.name: lc
values.expr: n1 if perm.c == 1 else (n2 if perm.c == 2 else (n3 if perm.c == 3 else n4))

values.name: ld
values.expr: n1 if perm.d == 1 else (n2 if perm.d == 2 else (n3 if perm.d == 3 else n4))

patterns.text: Four buses have travelled A: {la:num} km, B: {lb:num} km, C: {lc:num} km and D: {ld:num} km. Which shows the buses from the shortest to the longest distance?

wrong.mistake: arranges from the longest to the shortest
compares only the last three digits and ignores the thousands
compares the ones digit before the tens digit

patterns.hint: Compare the thousands first, then the hundreds, then the tens.
patterns.explanation: {n1:num} is the shortest because it has fewer thousands. Then {n2:num} < {n3:num} < {n4:num}, so the order is {perm.ok}.
patterns.misconception: Compares only the first visible digit rather than number of digits and left-to-right place value.
patterns.notes: Four readings built like 18,990; 19,009; 19,090; 19,900: one with a smaller thousands part but many big digits, and three that share their thousands and differ only in where one digit (2 to 9) sits. Thousands part 11 to 98; 8 different letter arrangements.

patterns.text: Arrange {na:num}; {ne:num}; {nc:num}; {nd:num}; {nb:num} from smallest to greatest. Which number is in the middle?

steps.text: Picks the third of the five, {mid:num}.

patterns.hint: The middle of five ordered numbers is the third number.
patterns.explanation: The order is {nd:num}; {small:num}; {mid:num}; {big:num}; {ne:num}. The middle number is {mid:num}.
patterns.misconception: Compares only the first visible digit rather than number of digits and left-to-right place value.
patterns.notes: Three numbers share a thousands part (11 to 97 thousand) and use the same three different digits in other orders; one has one thousand less and one has one thousand more. The middle number is never the third one listed.

patterns.text: Swap the digits {dp} and {dq} in {n:num}. What number is formed?
patterns.hint: Only the places of {dp} and {dq} change. The other digits stay where they are.
patterns.explanation: The {dp} and the {dq} change places and the other digits stay, so {n:num} becomes {ans:num}.
patterns.misconception: Creates a leading zero or changes more than the allowed digits.
patterns.notes: n: 10,000 to 99,999. The two digits swapped each appear only once in n, so the question is clear. Any two places from ten-thousands down to ones; a 0 is never moved to the ten-thousands place (no leading zero).

values.name: m1
values.expr: min(p if p != lo else 10, q if q != lo else 10, r if r != lo else 10, s if s != lo else 10)

values.name: m2
values.expr: p + q + r + s - lo - hi - m1

values.name: s3
values.expr: 0 if z == 3 else (q if z < 3 else r)

values.name: s4
values.expr: 0 if z == 4 else (r if z < 4 else s)

patterns.text: Using the digits {s1}, {s2}, {s3}, {s4} and {s5} once each, what is the smallest five-digit number you can make?

wrong.mistake: puts 0 first, which makes only a four-digit number
leaves the 0 in the ones place instead of the thousands place
puts 0 second but arranges the other digits from greatest to smallest

patterns.hint: A five-digit number cannot begin with 0.
patterns.explanation: Begin with the smallest non-zero digit {lo}, then 0, then {m1}, {m2} and {hi} from smallest to greatest: {small:num}.
patterns.misconception: Creates a leading zero or changes more than the allowed digits.
patterns.notes: Four different non-zero digits (1 to 9) and one 0, listed in a mixed order; the 0 is never listed first. Wrong options: 0 put first (a four-digit number), 0 put last, and 0 second with the rest in descending order.

values.name: m1
values.expr: min(p if p != lo else 10, q if q != lo else 10, r if r != lo else 10, s if s != lo else 10)

values.name: m2
values.expr: p + q + r + s - lo - hi - m1

values.name: s3
values.expr: 0 if z == 3 else (q if z < 3 else r)

values.name: s4
values.expr: 0 if z == 4 else (r if z < 4 else s)

patterns.text: Using the digits {s1}, {s2}, {s3}, {s4} and {s5} once each, make the greatest and the smallest five-digit numbers. Subtract the smallest from the greatest.

steps.text: Forms both numbers correctly: greatest {great:num} and smallest {small:num} (the smallest does not begin with 0).

patterns.hint: Form both numbers first. The smallest cannot begin with 0.
patterns.explanation: Greatest = {great:num} (digits from greatest to smallest). Smallest = {small:num} ({lo} first, then 0). Difference = {great:num} − {small:num} = {great - small:num}.
patterns.misconception: Creates a leading zero or changes more than the allowed digits.
patterns.notes: Four different non-zero digits (1 to 9) and one 0, listed in a mixed order with the 0 never first. The answer is always a positive five-digit number.

patterns.text: How many multiples of {u:num} lie strictly between {a:num} and {b:num}?
patterns.hint: Start with the first multiple of {u:num} after {a:num}.
patterns.explanation: The first multiple of {u:num} after {a:num} is {first:num}, and the last one before {b:num} is {last:num}. Counting {first:num}, {first + u:num}, … , {last:num} gives {count}.
patterns.misconception: Includes one or both boundary numbers when the wording says 'between'.
patterns.notes: Multiples of 100 or of 1,000. Both boundaries are multiples of 50 but never multiples of the number asked about, so no boundary question arises; the gap is 3 to 8 multiples wide (answer 3 to 8). Both numbers below 99,000.

patterns.text: A {ctx} number is greater than {a:num} but less than {b:num}. Which could it be?

wrong.mistake: includes the lower boundary number
includes the upper boundary number
checks only that the number is less than the upper boundary

patterns.hint: It must be more than {a:num} and also less than {b:num}.
patterns.explanation: {c:num} is greater than {a:num} and less than {b:num}. {a:num} and {b:num} are the boundaries themselves, and {a - j:num} is less than {a:num}.
patterns.misconception: Includes one or both boundary numbers when the wording says 'between'.
patterns.notes: Lower boundary 10,000 to 98,000 (a multiple of 10); the upper is 10, 20, 50 or 100 more. Wrong options: each boundary, and a number 1 to 9 below the lower boundary.

patterns.text: How many whole numbers lie strictly between {a:num} and {b:num}?

steps.text: Starts at {a + 1:num} and stops at {b - 1:num}, leaving out both boundary numbers.

patterns.hint: Do not count {a:num} or {b:num} themselves.
patterns.explanation: The numbers are {a + 1:num}, {a + 2:num}, … up to {b - 1:num}. That is {b:num} − {a:num} − 1 = {ans} numbers.
patterns.misconception: Includes one or both boundary numbers when the wording says 'between'.
patterns.notes: The two numbers sit 2 to 9 either side of a whole hundred or thousand (1,100 to 99,000), so the list crosses it, as in the bank's 5,996 and 6,002. Answer 3 to 17. Counting one boundary gives one more; counting both gives two more.

patterns.text: {ctx.lead} {n:num} {ctx.what}. Round this number to the nearest 10.
patterns.hint: Look at the ones digit.
patterns.explanation: The ones digit is {digit(n, 1)}, so {n:num} rounds {'up' if rn > n else 'down'} to {rn:num}.
patterns.misconception: Looks at the tens digit instead of the ones digit or rounds a 5 downward.
patterns.notes: n: 1,001 to 99,994, not a multiple of 10 (an ones digit of 5 rounds up).

patterns.text: The number of {ctx}, rounded to the nearest 10, is {rr:num}. Which could be the actual number?

wrong.mistake: rounds an ones digit of 5 down
drops the ones digit instead of rounding
rounds an ones digit of 4 up

patterns.hint: Which numbers round to {rr:num}? Think of the ones digit.
patterns.explanation: Numbers from {rr - 5:num} to {rr + 4:num} round to {rr:num}, and {c:num} is one of them. {rr + 5:num} and {rr + 7:num} round up to {rr + 10:num}; {rr - 6:num} rounds down to {rr - 10:num}.
patterns.misconception: Looks at the tens digit instead of the ones digit or rounds a 5 downward.
patterns.notes: Rounded count 1,010 to 99,980 (a multiple of 10). The right option is 5 below to 4 above it (never the rounded number itself). Wrong options: 5 above, 7 above, 6 below.

patterns.text: {ctx} carried {a:num} passengers in {mo.m1} and {b:num} in {mo.m2}. Round each number to the nearest 10, then add to estimate the total.
patterns.hint: Round each number first, then add.
patterns.explanation: {a:num} → {ra:num} and {b:num} → {rb:num}. Estimated total = {ra:num} + {rb:num} = {ra + rb:num}.
patterns.misconception: Looks at the tens digit instead of the ones digit or rounds a 5 downward.
patterns.notes: Two counts of 1,001 to 49,994, neither a multiple of 10; one rounds up and the other rounds down, so both directions are tested.

values.name: wrong_way
values.expr: down + 100 if right == down else down

patterns.text: Round {n:num} to the nearest 100.

wrong.mistake: rounds the wrong way
rounds to the nearest 10
rounds to the nearest 1,000

patterns.hint: Look at the tens digit.
patterns.explanation: The tens digit is {digit(n, 10)}, so {n:num} rounds {'up' if right > n else 'down'} to {right:num}.
patterns.misconception: Looks at the hundreds digit instead of the tens digit.
patterns.notes: n: 1,050 to 99,949, not a multiple of 100, and every wrong option different from the right one.

patterns.text: What is the {ask.word} whole number that rounds to {rr:num} to the nearest 100?
patterns.hint: Find the halfway numbers between {rr:num} and the hundreds on either side of it.
patterns.explanation: Numbers from {rr - 50:num} to {rr + 49:num} round to {rr:num}. The {ask.word} of them is {ans:num}.
patterns.misconception: Looks at the hundreds digit instead of the tens digit.
patterns.notes: Rounded number 1,100 to 99,800, a multiple of 100. Asks for the greatest (49 above) or the smallest (50 below, as 50 rounds up).

values.name: ctx
choice: bus tickets sold in a month
travellers at an airport in a day

patterns.text: The number of {ctx}, rounded to the nearest 100, is {rr:num}. Which could be the actual number?

wrong.mistake: rounds a final 50 down
keeps the same hundreds digit without looking at the tens digit
rounds a number below the halfway point up

patterns.hint: Look at the tens digit of each number.
patterns.explanation: Numbers from {rr - 50:num} to {rr + 49:num} round to {rr:num}, and {c:num} is one of them. {rr + 50:num} and {rr + t:num} round up to {rr + 100:num}; {rr - w:num} rounds down to {rr - 100:num}.
patterns.misconception: Looks at the hundreds digit instead of the tens digit.
patterns.notes: Rounded count 1,100 to 99,800 (a multiple of 100). The right option is 50 below to 49 above it (never the rounded number itself). Wrong options: exactly 50 above, 51 to 99 above (same hundreds digit, rounds up), 51 to 99 below.

patterns.text: Which number gives the same answer when rounded to the nearest 100 and to the nearest 1,000?

wrong.mistake: rounds only to the nearest 1,000 and does not check the nearest 100
looks at the hundreds digit 4 instead of the tens digit, so rounds down to the hundred as well
rounds only to the nearest 100 and does not check the nearest 1,000

steps.text: Rounds the numbers to the nearest 100 correctly (for example {wb:num} → {round_half_up(wb, 100):num}).
Compares with the nearest 1,000 and chooses {cor:num}, which gives {r:num} both ways.

patterns.hint: Round each number to the nearest 100 and then to the nearest 1,000.
patterns.explanation: {cor:num} rounds to {r:num} both ways. {wa:num} gives {round_half_up(wa, 100):num} and {round_half_up(wa, 1000):num}; {wb:num} gives {round_half_up(wb, 100):num} and {round_half_up(wb, 1000):num}; {we:num} gives {round_half_up(we, 100):num} and {round_half_up(we, 1000):num}.
patterns.misconception: Looks at the hundreds digit instead of the tens digit.
patterns.notes: All four options are in the same thousand (2,000s to 98,000s). The right one ends in 001 to 049 or in 951 to 999. Wrong ones end in 150 to 449, in 450 to 499 (hundreds digit 4 but rounds up to 500), or in 510 to 940.

patterns.text: {ctx.lead} {n:num} km {ctx.tail}. Round this distance to the nearest 1,000 km.
patterns.hint: Compare the number with the halfway number between the two thousands.
patterns.explanation: {n:num} lies between {lo:num} and {lo + 1000:num}. The halfway number is {lo + 500:num}, and {n:num} is {'above' if n > lo + 500 else ('equal to' if n == lo + 500 else 'below')} it, so it rounds to {rn:num} km.
patterns.misconception: Uses the thousands digit to decide instead of comparing with the midpoint.
patterns.notes: n: 1,001 to 99,999 km, not a whole thousand (a number from 99,500 rounds to 1,00,000 = 100,000). The unit km is stated in the question.

patterns.text: {who.name} rounded {n:num} to the nearest 1,000 and got {learner:num}. What is the correct answer?

wrong.mistake: decides by the thousands digit, as the learner did, instead of comparing with the halfway number
rounds to the nearest 100 instead
gives the halfway number instead of a whole thousand

patterns.hint: Compare {n:num} with the halfway number {mid:num}.
patterns.explanation: {n:num} is {'above' if n > mid else 'below'} the halfway number {mid:num}, so it rounds {'up' if rn > n else 'down'} to {rn:num}. The thousands digit, {digit(n, 1000)}, does not decide this.
patterns.misconception: Uses the thousands digit to decide instead of comparing with the midpoint.
patterns.notes: n: 1,001 to 98,999, not a whole hundred. The learner's answer always comes from deciding by the thousands digit (5 or more up), and only numbers where that gives the wrong answer are used. Wrong options: the learner's answer, the nearest 100, the halfway number.

patterns.text: {ctx.place} had {a:num} {ctx.what} in {mo.m1} and {b:num} in {mo.m2}. Round each number to the nearest 1,000 and estimate how many more came in {mo.m2}.
patterns.hint: Round each number first, then subtract.
patterns.explanation: {a:num} → {ra:num} and {b:num} → {rb:num}. About {rb:num} − {ra:num} = {rb - ra:num} more {ctx.what} came in {mo.m2}.
patterns.misconception: Uses the thousands digit to decide instead of comparing with the midpoint.
patterns.notes: First count 10,001 to 60,000; the second is 3,000 to 35,000 more (at most 95,000). Neither is a whole thousand; one rounds up and the other down.

patterns.competency: Estimation of a school-based large count
patterns.text: {c.s1} {a} {c.g} with about {b} {c.s2}. Round both numbers to the nearest 10 and estimate the total number of {c.what}.
patterns.hint: Round {a} and {b} to the nearest 10 first, then multiply.
patterns.explanation: {a} is about {ra} and {b} is about {rb}, so the estimate is {ra} × {rb} = {ra * rb:num} {c.what}.
patterns.misconception: Treats an estimate as an exact answer or chooses units that are not plausible.
patterns.notes: Two numbers from 21 to 89 and 21 to 79, neither ending in 0 or 5 (so the rounding is never a tie and is always needed). Answer: the product of the rounded numbers (400 to 7,200). Four contexts: hall seats, school students, library books, train passengers.

patterns.text: Which is the best quick estimate for {a} × {b}?

wrong.mistake: loses a zero when multiplying the rounded numbers
writes one zero too many when multiplying the rounded numbers
adds the rounded numbers instead of multiplying them

patterns.hint: Round {a} to the nearest 100 and {b} to the nearest 10.
patterns.explanation: {a} is about {h * 100} and {b} is about {t * 10}, so a quick estimate is {h * 100} × {t * 10} = {est:num}.
patterns.misconception: Treats an estimate as an exact answer or chooses units that are not plausible.
patterns.notes: First number within 4 of a hundred from 200 to 900 (never the hundred itself); second within 2 of a ten from 20 to 90 (never the ten itself). Right answer: the product of the rounded numbers (4,000 to 81,000). Wrong options: one zero fewer, one zero more, the rounded numbers added.

patterns.text: Estimate the {op.word} {x:num} {op.sign} {y:num} by rounding both numbers to the nearest 1,000.
patterns.hint: Look at the hundreds digit of each number to round it to the nearest 1,000.
patterns.explanation: {x:num} rounds to {rx:num} and {y:num} rounds to {ry:num}. So the estimate is {rx:num} {op.sign} {ry:num} = {ans:num}.

steps.text: Rounds both numbers to the nearest 1,000: {x:num} to {rx:num} and {y:num} to {ry:num}.

patterns.misconception: Treats an estimate as an exact answer or chooses units that are not plausible.
patterns.notes: A sum or a difference of two 5-digit numbers. First number 20,000 to 89,999; second 10,000 up to 3,000 less than the first, and for a sum small enough that the two add to at most 99,999. Neither number is a whole thousand or ends in exactly 500 (no ties). Answer: the rounded sum or difference.

patterns.text: {who.name} {mode.verb} at {speed} km each hour. How far does {who.he} go in {hours} hours at the same speed?
patterns.hint: The same distance is covered in every hour.
patterns.explanation: {speed} km each hour for {hours} hours is {speed} × {hours} = {speed * hours} km.
patterns.misconception: Adds the rate once instead of multiplying by the number of equal intervals.
patterns.notes: Walking 3 to 6 km an hour, cycling 8 to 20, a bus 30 to 60; 2 to 6 hours. The answer is in km, stated in the question.

patterns.text: A {v.one} covers {total} km in {hours} hours, going the same distance each hour. How many kilometres does it cover each hour?
patterns.hint: Share the total distance equally among the {hours} hours.
patterns.explanation: {total} ÷ {hours} = {speed}, so the {v.one} covers {speed} km each hour.
patterns.misconception: Adds the rate once instead of multiplying by the number of equal intervals.
patterns.notes: A train 40 to 90 km each hour, a bus 30 to 60, a ferry 12 to 30, a truck 30 to 55; 2 to 8 hours. The total is the speed times the hours, so the answer is always a whole number of km, stated in the question.

patterns.text: A {v.one} covers {s} km in the first hour and the same distance in each of the next {n} hours. How many kilometres does it travel in all?

wrong.mistake: leaves out the first hour and multiplies by the next hours only
adds the distance and the number of hours instead of multiplying
counts the first hour twice

patterns.hint: Count all the hours: the first hour and the next {n}.
patterns.explanation: There are 1 + {n} = {n + 1} hours altogether, so the {v.one} travels {s} × {n + 1} = {s * (n + 1)} km.
patterns.misconception: Adds the rate once instead of multiplying by the number of equal intervals.
patterns.notes: A train 50 to 90 km in an hour, a bus 30 to 60, a truck 35 to 60; 2 to 6 further hours. Right answer: the distance times all the hours. Wrong options: the first hour left out, distance and hours added, the first hour counted twice.

patterns.text: A {v.one} travels {s} km each hour. After {h} hours, it still has {left} km to go. How long is the whole route?
patterns.hint: First find how far the {v.one} has already gone, then add the part still to go.
patterns.explanation: In {h} hours the {v.one} goes {s} × {h} = {done} km. The whole route is {done} + {left} = {done + left} km.

steps.text: Finds the distance already covered: {s} × {h} = {done} km.
Adds the distance still to go: {done} + {left} = {done + left} km.

patterns.misconception: Adds the rate once instead of multiplying by the number of equal intervals.
patterns.notes: A bus 35 to 65 km each hour, a train 50 to 90, a truck 40 to 60; 3 to 7 hours; 12 to 99 km still to go. Answer in km, stated in the question.

patterns.text: {children} children are going on a school trip. Each {vehicle.one} can carry {cap} children. How many {vehicle.many} are needed so that every child goes?
patterns.hint: What happens to the children left over after the full {vehicle.many}?
patterns.explanation: {full} full {vehicle.many} carry {cap * full} children; the {extra} left over need one more, so {full + 1} {vehicle.many}.
patterns.misconception: Drops the remainder even when every person or object must be accommodated.
patterns.notes: A van carries 8 to 12, a bus 30 to 45, an auto-rickshaw 3 or 4; 2 to 6 full vehicles plus one part-full (never an exact fit).

patterns.text: A school hires {n} {v.many} for a trip. Each {v.one} has {c} seats. How many seats are there altogether?
patterns.hint: Multiply the number of {v.many} by the seats in each {v.one}.
patterns.explanation: {n} {v.many} with {c} seats each have {n} × {c} = {n * c:num} seats.
patterns.misconception: Drops the remainder even when every person or object must be accommodated.
patterns.notes: 5 to 15 vehicles: a bus with 30 to 52 seats, a van 8 to 14, a coach 40 to 56, a boat 6 to 20. Answer: vehicles times seats (30 to 840).

patterns.text: {p} students go on a trip in {v.many} that each seat {cap}. The {v.many} are filled one by one. How many seats are empty in the last {v.one}?

wrong.mistake: gives the number of students in the last vehicle instead of the empty seats
gives the number of full vehicles
gives the number of vehicles needed

patterns.hint: Find how many students are left over after the full {v.many}.
patterns.explanation: {p} ÷ {cap} = {q} remainder {rem}. The last {v.one} has {rem} {'student' if rem == 1 else 'students'}, so {cap} − {rem} = {cap - rem} {'seat' if (cap - rem) == 1 else 'seats'} are empty.
patterns.misconception: Drops the remainder even when every person or object must be accommodated.
patterns.notes: A van seats 8 to 12, a bus 30 to 45, a boat 10 to 20, a minibus 15 to 25; 3 to 9 full vehicles plus one part-full (never an exact fit). Right answer: the seats left in the part-full vehicle. Wrong options come from the same division: the remainder, the full vehicles, the vehicles needed; all four always differ.

patterns.text: A camp has {a} children and {b} adults. Each {v.one} seats {cap} people. How many {v.many} are needed to take everyone?
patterns.hint: Add the children and adults first, then think about the people left over.
patterns.explanation: {a} + {b} = {t} people. {need - 1} {v.many} seat {(need - 1) * cap} people, leaving {t % cap}, so {need} {v.many} are needed.

steps.text: Divides by {cap} ({need - 1} remainder {t % cap}) and adds one more for the {t % cap} left over: {need} {v.many}.

patterns.misconception: Drops the remainder even when every person or object must be accommodated.
patterns.notes: 120 to 360 children and 12 to 48 adults. A bus seats 35 to 50, a coach 40 to 56, a minibus 20 to 30. The total never fills the vehicles exactly, so the answer is always one more than the full vehicles (3 to 21).

patterns.text: Complete: {n:num} = {t} {'thousand' if t == 1 else 'thousands'} + ___ hundreds + {te} {'ten' if te == 1 else 'tens'} + {on} {'one' if on == 1 else 'ones'}.
patterns.hint: Take away {t * 1000:num}, {te * 10} and {on} from {n:num}, then count what is left in hundreds.
patterns.explanation: {n:num} − {t * 1000:num} − {te * 10} − {on} = {ans * 100:num}, which is {ans} hundreds.
patterns.misconception: Reports the digit in a place instead of the number of complete groups in the whole quantity.
patterns.notes: A 4-digit number 2,000 to 9,999 with no 0 in the tens or ones place. The thousands given are fewer than its thousands digit, so the missing hundreds are always 10 or more (never just the hundreds digit).

patterns.text: {who.name} says {n:num} has {d} complete {pl.one if d == 1 else pl.word}, because its {pl.word} digit is {d}. How many complete {pl.word} are there in {n:num}?

wrong.mistake: gives the digit in that place instead of the complete groups in the whole number
counts the complete groups of the next place up
counts the complete groups of the next place down

patterns.hint: Only complete groups count, and the larger places can be regrouped into {pl.word} too.
patterns.explanation: {n:num} = {right:num} × {pl.v:num} + {n % pl.v}, so there are {right:num} complete {pl.word}, not {d}.
patterns.misconception: Reports the digit in a place instead of the number of complete groups in the whole quantity.
patterns.notes: Complete hundreds in a number from 1,000 to 99,999, or complete thousands in one from 10,000 to 99,999. Right answer: the number divided by 100 or 1,000, remainder dropped. The place digit is never 0. Wrong options: the place digit (the skill's misconception), the groups of the next place up and down; all four always differ.

patterns.responseFormat: Quotient and remainder separated by a semicolon
patterns.text: {who.name} wants to change {amt:money} into {note:money} notes. How many complete notes can {who.he} get, and how many rupees are left over? Enter notes;rupees left.
patterns.hint: Find the greatest multiple of {note} that is not more than {amt:num}.
patterns.explanation: {q:num} × {note} = {q * note:num}, and one more note would need {(q + 1) * note:num}. So {who.he} gets {q:num} notes and {amt:money} − {q * note:money} = {r:money} is left.

steps.text: Finds the complete notes: {q:num} × {note} = {q * note:num}, and {q + 1} notes would need {(q + 1) * note:num}, which is too much. So {q:num} notes.
Finds what is left: {amt:num} − {q * note:num} = {r} {'rupee' if (r) == 1 else 'rupees'}.

patterns.misconception: Reports the digit in a place instead of the number of complete groups in the whole quantity.
patterns.notes: An amount from ₹5,000 to ₹99,999 changed into ₹200 or ₹500 notes, never an exact number of notes. Two boxes: the complete notes (10 to 499) and the rupees left (1 to 499).

patterns.text: A {sh.name} border has {k} {obj} on each side, including one at every corner. How many {obj} are there in all?
patterns.hint: Each corner one is counted on two sides.
patterns.explanation: Adding the sides gives {sh.sides} × {k} = {sh.sides * k}, but the {sh.sides} corner {obj} were counted twice. So there are {sh.sides * k} − {sh.sides} = {sh.sides * (k - 1)} {obj}.
patterns.misconception: Counts a shared object more than once or tests cases without preserving the puzzle rule.
patterns.notes: A triangle, square, pentagon or hexagon with 3 to 12 objects on each side, corners included. Answer: sides × (objects on a side − 1).

patterns.text: Make a two-digit number with the digits {a} and {b}, then swap its digits to make a second number. Subtract the smaller number from the larger. What is the difference?

wrong.mistake: takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of regrouping
adds the two numbers instead of subtracting
subtracts the two digits instead of the two numbers

patterns.hint: The two numbers are {big} and {small}.
patterns.explanation: The numbers are {big} and {small}, and {big} − {small} = {big - small}.
patterns.misconception: Counts a shared object more than once or tests cases without preserving the puzzle rule.
patterns.notes: Two different digits from 1 to 9 (no 0, so both numbers are two-digit). Right answer: 9 × the difference of the digits. Wrong options: column-by-column subtraction without regrouping, the sum of the numbers, the difference of the digits.

patterns.text: A rectangular border has {l} {obj} on each long side and {s} on each short side, counting the {obj} at all four corners. How many {obj} are there in all?
patterns.hint: Add all four sides, then think about the corners.
patterns.explanation: The four sides add up to {l} + {l} + {s} + {s} = {sides}. Each of the 4 corner {obj} was counted on two sides, so there are {sides} − 4 = {sides - 4} {obj}.

steps.text: Takes away the 4 corner {obj} counted twice: {sides} − 4 = {sides - 4}.

patterns.misconception: Counts a shared object more than once or tests cases without preserving the puzzle rule.
patterns.notes: Long sides 5 to 15 objects, short sides 3 up to one fewer than the long side, corners included. Answer: twice each side added, minus 4.

parts.text: (a) How many people are going on the trip in all?
parts.explanation: {students} + {teachers} = {total} people.

parts.text: (b) How many buses are needed so that everyone goes?
parts.explanation: {total} ÷ {cap} = {q} remainder {r}. The {r} people left over need one more bus, so {buses} buses.

parts.text: (c) How many seats will be empty on these buses?
parts.explanation: {buses} × {cap} = {buses * cap} seats, and {buses * cap} − {total} = {empty} are empty.

patterns.stimulus: A newspaper says that {r:num} people {event}. The number was rounded to the nearest {u:num}. Answer each step in its own box.

parts.text: (a) What is the smallest number of people who could have come?
parts.explanation: {lo:num} is halfway between {r - u:num} and {r:num}, and a halfway number rounds up, so it rounds to {r:num}; {lo - 1:num} would round to {r - u:num}.

parts.text: (b) What is the greatest number of people who could have come?
parts.explanation: {hi + 1:num} would round up to {r + u:num}, so the greatest is {hi:num}.

parts.text: (c) How many different exact numbers of people are possible?
parts.explanation: From {lo:num} to {hi:num} there are {hi:num} − {lo:num} + 1 = {hi - lo + 1:num} numbers.

patterns.misconception: Uses the thousands digit to decide instead of comparing with the midpoint.
patterns.notes: Rounded to the nearest 1,000 (a thousand from 12,000 to 98,000) or the nearest 100 (a hundred from 1,200 to 9,800). The smallest is half the unit below, the greatest one less than half the unit above, so 1,000 or 100 numbers are possible. Step question (#208): (a) smallest, (b) greatest, (c) how many.

patterns.stimulus: {who.name} has five number cards: {d3 if order == 1 else d2}, 0, {d1 if order == 1 else d4}, {d4 if order == 1 else (d3 if order == 2 else d1)}, {d2 if order == 1 else (d1 if order == 2 else d3)}. Using each card once, {who.he} makes 5-digit numbers. Answer each step in its own box.

parts.text: (a) What is the greatest 5-digit number {who.he} can make?
parts.explanation: Biggest digits in the highest places and 0 in the ones place: {big:num}.

parts.text: (b) What is the smallest 5-digit number {who.he} can make?
parts.explanation: A 5-digit number cannot start with 0, so it starts with {d1}, then 0, then {d2}, {d3}, {d4}: {small:num}.

parts.text: (c) What is the difference between the greatest and the smallest of these numbers?
parts.explanation: {big:num} − {small:num} = {big - small:num}.

patterns.misconception: Creates a leading zero or changes more than the allowed digits.
patterns.notes: Four different digits from 1 to 9 plus a 0, shown in one of three mixed-up orders. The smallest number always has 0 in the thousands place. Step question (#208): (a) greatest, (b) smallest, (c) difference.

patterns.stimulus: {who.name}'s family drives {d} km to {who.his} {dest}. Before lunch they drive at {s1} km each hour for {h1} hours. After lunch they drive at {s2} km each hour until they reach. Answer each step in its own box.

parts.text: (a) How far do they drive before lunch?
(b) How far is left to drive after lunch?
parts.explanation: {d} − {m} = {rest} km.

parts.text: (c) For how many hours do they drive after lunch?
parts.explanation: {rest} ÷ {s2} = {h2} hours.

parts.text: (d) For how many hours do they drive in all?

patterns.misconception: Adds the rate once instead of multiplying by the number of equal intervals.
patterns.notes: Before lunch 40 to 65 km an hour for 2 to 4 hours; after lunch 30 to 60 km an hour (a multiple of 5) for 2 to 5 hours, so the distance left always divides exactly. The two speeds differ and the two times differ. Journey 110 to 560 km. Step question (#208): (a) distance before lunch, (b) distance left, (c) hours after lunch (2 marks, all or nothing), (d) total hours.

patterns.stimulus: Each of the {n} children in Class 5 pays {p:money} for a school trip to {trip}. Their teacher, {who.name}, takes all the money to the bank and asks for as many ₹500 notes as possible, then as many ₹100 notes as possible, and the rest in ₹10 notes. Answer each step in its own box.

parts.explanation: {n} × {p:money} = {t:money}.

parts.text: (b) How many ₹500 notes does {who.he} get?
parts.explanation: {t:num} ÷ 500 = {n500} remainder {r500}, so {n500} notes of ₹500.

parts.text: (c) How many ₹100 notes does {who.he} get?

parts.text: (d) How many ₹10 notes does {who.he} get?
parts.explanation: After the ₹100 notes, {r500 % 100:money} is left: {n10} notes of ₹10.

Step question (#208): (a) total (2 marks, all or nothing), (b) ₹500 notes, (c) ₹100 notes, (d) ₹10 notes. The ₹100 and ₹10 counts always differ.

patterns.stimulus: A {train} has {c} coaches. Each coach has {s} seats. Answer each step in its own box.

parts.explanation: {s} rounds to {rs}.

parts.text: (d) By how many seats does the estimate differ from the exact number?
parts.explanation: The estimate {est:num} is {gap} {way} than the exact {ex:num}.

patterns.stimulus: Case study: The number of visitors to {site} on four days of the Dussehra holidays was: Monday {mon:num}, Tuesday {tue:num}, Wednesday {wed:num} and Thursday {thu:num}.

parts.text: (a) On which day did the most visitors come?

wrong.mistake: compares only the first digit and picks the 4-digit number
picks the second greatest number
picks the smallest 5-digit number

parts.hint: First count the digits in each number.
parts.explanation: {small:num} has only 4 digits, so it is the smallest. Of the 5-digit numbers, {g:num} is the greatest, so the most visitors came on {dg}.

parts.text: (b) Write the four numbers of visitors in order from the smallest to the greatest.
parts.hint: A 4-digit number is smaller than any 5-digit number. Then compare the 5-digit numbers place by place from the left.
parts.explanation: {small:num} < {lo:num} < {mid:num} < {g:num}.

parts.text: (c) How many more visitors came on {dg} than on {ds}?

patterns.stimulus: Case study: For Diwali, Class 5 is placing diyas along the edges of a square stage. Each side has {n} diyas, counting the diyas at both corners of that side. {who.name} adds the four sides and says that {4 * n} diyas are needed.

parts.explanation: Adding the four sides counts each of the 4 corner diyas twice, so {4 * n} − 4 = {real} diyas.

parts.text: (b) What mistake did {who.name} make?

parts.text: (d) What is the difference between the estimate and the exact total?
parts.hint: Subtract the smaller total from the bigger one.
parts.explanation: {max(est, ex):num} − {min(est, ex):num} = {abs(est - ex)}. The estimate is {'more' if est > ex else 'less'} than the exact total.

patterns.misconception: Looks at the hundreds digit instead of the tens digit.
patterns.notes: Three 4-digit counts from 1,050 to 9,949; none ends in 00 or 50, so no count is exactly halfway. The wrong options in (a) all differ from the right answer, and the estimate is never exactly the total.
